Carbon Prices Cut Emissions

What Ten Natural Experiments Show About Fuel Taxes, Carbon Prices and Subsidy Reform

Published

November 2026

Abstract

Ministries weighing a carbon tax are usually shown a model’s estimate of what it will do. This brief reports what happened instead, in ten cases where a carbon tax, a fuel tax, an emissions trading price, a subsidy cut or a price shock raised fuel prices and researchers later measured the effect. Every case shows a cut. In road transport and home heating, sustained prices cut emissions from the priced fuels by about 1 to 2 percent for each 10 dollars a tonne, building up over five to fifteen years. In power, where gas plants could replace coal, the cut per dollar was five to ten times larger. Taxes moved demand more than equal market price changes, while offsetting tax cuts, exemptions and unpriced coal weakened the effect. Ministries can plan on these magnitudes, and modelers should test their tools against these cases.

Keywords

carbon tax, natural experiment, ex post evaluation, fuel prices, emissions trading, subsidy reform

Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.5, November 2026. Draft for review. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The ten case studies, with each case’s price path over time, the conversions and the evidence register, are in the working paper.

Key messages

Read the full working paper → · Download this brief (pdf)

Carbon prices have cut emissions in every case where the effect was properly measured. Ten natural experiments, from Sweden in 1991 to Germany in 2022, in road transport, buildings, industry and power, all show cuts in the fuels that were priced.

In transport and heating, expect about 1 to 2 percent less use for each 10 dollars a tonne, building up over five to fifteen years. Germany’s eco-tax, worth about €65 a tonne by 2003, cut transport emissions by 11 to 16 percent by 2005.

In power, where gas plants could replace coal, the cut per dollar was five to ten times larger. Britain’s carbon price floor took coal from 39 percent of generation in 2012 to 2 percent in 2019 and cut power-sector emissions by about a fifth a year.

How the price is designed matters as much as its level. Taxes moved demand more than equal market price changes; offsetting tax cuts, exemptions and unpriced coal weakened the effect.

Use these cases to test the models. On this evidence the Climate Policy Assessment Tool’s long-run response for gasoline is about right, its response for home heating looks too high, and it applies the response too early.

What happened when fuel prices rose

Most estimates of what a carbon tax will do come from models; these ten cases show what real price rises did. In each, a government or a market raised fuel prices for reasons largely independent of the emissions trend. Researchers later compared emissions or fuel use with a credible estimate of what would otherwise have happened: usually a weighted average of similar countries or provinces without the policy, or similar plants outside the scheme. Each case is reported the same way: how far the measure raised prices, its carbon price or its dollar-per-tonne equivalent, and the measured cut (Table 1).

The evidence is strongest for Sweden, Germany’s eco-tax, Britain’s power sector and the EU trading system. Each rests on peer-reviewed studies that compare the treated country or plants with close comparators, and Sweden’s headline result has been reproduced independently (Andersson 2019; Bonander et al. 2023; Yu 2024). The Swiss and Indonesian estimates lean partly on modeled counterfactuals and are backed by household or panel studies (Federal Office for the Environment 2018; Francescutto and Mathys 2022; Burke and Kurniawati 2018). Eleven further episodes, including Australia’s 2012–2014 carbon price and Finland’s early carbon tax, point the same way but rest on thinner evidence (working paper, cases left out).

Transport and heating: about 1 to 2 percent per 10 dollars a tonne

Sustained prices on road fuels and heating cut their use by roughly 1 to 2 percent for each 10 dollars a tonne within five to fifteen years. Germany’s eco-tax, worth about €65 a tonne on petrol by 2003, cut transport emissions by 11 to 16 percent by 2005 (Runst and Höhle 2022). Sweden’s carbon tax cut transport emissions by about 6 percent on its own (Andersson 2019). Switzerland’s heating levy cut heating-fuel emissions by 4 to 10 percent by 2015, and house owners’ heating fuel by 12 to 14 percent once the levy passed CHF 60 a tonne (Federal Office for the Environment 2018; Francescutto and Mathys 2022). In the United States a 10-cent state tax rise, worth about 11 dollars a tonne, cut gasoline use by about 1.4 percent within a single year (Davis and Kilian 2011). Figure 1 plots every case against its price.

The response builds over years because cars and boilers last. Drivers and households cut back a little at once, but most of the saving comes as vehicles, boilers and heating systems are replaced. German fuel use fell only after three to four years, and British Columbia’s long-run cut in transport emissions is about four times its short-run cut (Runst and Höhle 2022; Pretis 2022).

Very large, short price shocks buy less per dollar. Germany’s 2022 gas crisis raised household gas prices by 130 percent and industrial prices nearly sixfold, a carbon-price equivalent of hundreds of dollars a tonne, yet gas use fell by about a quarter (Ruhnau et al. 2023). Indonesia’s 89 percent gasoline price rise cut toll-road traffic by 10 percent within two years (Burke et al. 2017). Within months people can turn down the heating, but they cannot yet replace the boiler.

Power: much more per dollar where gas can replace coal

A modest carbon price emptied Britain’s coal plants because gas plants were standing by. From 2013 Britain added a tax on fuels for power generation to the EU allowance price, for a total of 14 to 36 dollars a tonne. A coal plant emits about 2.4 times as much CO₂ per unit of electricity as a gas plant, so the tax raised coal plants’ fuel costs by up to 141 percent and gas plants’ by up to 30 percent. Coal’s share of generation fell from 39 percent in 2012 to 9 percent in 2016 and 2 percent in 2019, and power-sector emissions were 20 to 26 percent lower each year over 2013–2017 (Leroutier 2022). Counting only the switch at plants that stayed open, the cut was 6 percent, at an average cost of €18 a tonne (Abrell et al. 2022).

The EU trading system cut emissions at regulated plants by about a tenth at prices near 14 euros. Comparisons of regulated with similar unregulated plants find cuts of 10 to 16 percent in its first two phases, with no measurable loss of output or jobs (Dechezleprêtre et al. 2023; Colmer et al. 2025). The cut was large for the price, which suggests firms responded to the expected tightening of the cap as much as to the price of the day (Bayer and Aklin 2020).

Design matters as much as the price

Taxes moved demand two to three times more than equal market price changes. British Columbia’s carbon tax cut household gasoline use 2.9 times as much as an equal market price rise, and the ratio was about three in Sweden and the United States (Lawley and Thivierge 2018; Andersson 2019; Li et al. 2014). Taxes are announced, expected to last and talked about. Part of the gap is drivers buying ahead of announced rises, and it fades over time (Coglianese et al. 2017; Erutku and Hildebrand 2018).

Offsetting tax cuts, exemptions and unpriced coal weakened the effect. Sweden cut its energy tax on petrol while it more than doubled the carbon tax in 2001–2004, and the gap in transport emissions barely widened (Andersson 2019). British Columbia cut transport emissions but not, measurably, its total emissions (Pretis 2022). Germany’s 2022 gas shock cut gas use by 23 percent, but national emissions fell only 1.3 percent because power stations burned more coal and some industry moved abroad (Umweltbundesamt 2024; Moll et al. 2023).

What to do

Finance ministries: plan on about 1 to 2 percent fewer emissions per 10 dollars a tonne in transport and buildings, building up over a decade. A sustained price of 50 dollars a tonne on road fuels and heating should cut their emissions by roughly 5 to 10 percent within ten years. Revenue erodes slowly, which helps the budget. In power systems with idle gas or renewable capacity, a price of 20 to 40 dollars a tonne can cut power-sector emissions by a fifth within five years.

Price the substitutes together, and do not offset the price elsewhere. Price coal alongside gas, avoid exemptions for the users who can respond most, and do not cut other fuel taxes as the carbon price rises. A published, rising schedule, like Switzerland’s automatic increases, does more than unannounced changes of the same size.

Modelers: back-cast these cases. On this evidence the Climate Policy Assessment Tool’s long-run gasoline elasticity, −0.64, is about right. Its −0.70 for natural gas in homes is above the −0.15 to −0.45 that the heating cases imply, and it applies the full response in the first year (Brief 5.4). Give each model the data from before the policy and the prices that followed, and compare its predicted cut with the measured one, as Brief 5.3 proposes.
